issues.legal_issue: A statutory tenure that preserves only the assessment then payable limits the government’s power to enhance land revenue.
material_facts: The land was held under a tenure governed by legislation that extinguished the former landlord’s rights while preserving the rents then payable and providing that they would continue to be payable.
The assessment payable when the legislation took effect was collected at the same rate until the land was acquired.
issues.conclusion: The tenure legislation limited the government’s right to assess the land to the assessment then payable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Foras Land Act, 1851 preserved the rents then payable and stated that they would continue to be payable; read together, those words limited the assessment rather than merely preserving an unlimited right to collect revenue. Section 4, which preserved liability to further general taxes, did not negate that limit. The general observation in Shapurji Jivanji v. Collector of Bombay that assessments on such land could be enhanced did not govern the specific statutory limit established here.

predicates.land_revenue_assessment_dispute: A dispute concerns the government’s assessment of land to revenue.
predicates.statutory_tenure_preserves_only_existing: The governing tenure instrument preserves only the assessment already payable and provides that it will continue to be payable.
predicates.statutory_tenure_expressly_limits_assess: The governing tenure instrument expressly places a limit on the assessment the government may levy.
predicates.assessment_limited_to_preserved_rate: The government may assess the land only up to the rate preserved by the tenure.

issues.definition: When a land-revenue assessment dispute concerns a tenure that preserves or expressly limits the existing assessment, the assessment is limited to the preserved rate.

issues.legal_issue: Acquiring private interests in land does not extinguish the government’s pre-existing sovereign power to assess the land to revenue.
material_facts: The government acquired the land for a public purpose under acquisition legislation.
The acquisition award valued and compensated the occupants’ interests in the land but did not value or award compensation for the government’s power to assess it.
After acquisition, the land vested absolutely in the government.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition extinguished the occupants’ rights in the land but did not acquire or extinguish the government’s right to assess it.
issues.legal_principle: Section VIII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1857 vested land in the government free from other estates, rights, titles and interests, meaning interests other than those already belonging to the government. The government acquires outstanding private interests, not its own interests or its sovereign prerogative to tax land. The Court agreed with the reasoning in In the Matter of the Land Acquisition Act: The Government of Bombay v. Esupali Salebhai and Deputy Collector, Calicut Division v. Aiyavu Pillay. The structure of the later Land Acquisition Act, 1894—particularly sections 3(b), 9, 11 and 16—also illustrated the distinction between compensable interests in land and the government’s assessment power.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a government acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.government_had_preexisting_assessment_po: The government had a power to assess the land to revenue before acquiring it.
predicates.acquisition_award_addressed_private_inte: The acquisition award valued or compensated private interests in the land without valuing or compensating the government’s assessment power.
predicates.government_assessment_power_survives_acq: The acquisition does not extinguish the government’s pre-existing power to assess the land.

issues.definition: When a public-purpose land acquisition concerns land that the government could already assess and the award addresses only private interests, the government’s assessment power survives the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: An absolute transfer of land by the Crown does not, without more, grant an exemption from land revenue.
material_facts: The Crown transferred the land by deed without stating that it was revenue-free.
The deed made the transfer subject to taxes, rates and assessments payable then or in the future.
There was no separate promise or representation establishing that the land would be exempt from assessment.
issues.conclusion: The transfer did not exempt the land from assessment; the deed’s terms subjected it to assessments, and an absolute sale alone did not imply a revenue exemption.
issues.legal_principle: A Crown grantee receives only what the grant conveys, and nothing passes by implication; the grant is construed by ascertaining the grantor’s intention from the deed’s language. Section 3 of the Crown Grants Act, 1895 applies to provisions, restrictions, conditions and limitations over whose validity might otherwise be affected by the Transfer of Property Act; it does not make an absolute grant revenue-free by implication. Thakur Jagannath Baksh Singh v. The United Provinces supports reading section 3 in light of the Act’s context. Dadoba v. Collector of Bombay rested on estoppel or a collateral contract arising from particular correspondence and deed terms, not on the absolute character of a sale alone. Lord v. Sydney supports construing grants according to their words and intention.

predicates.crown_grant_interpretation: The issue is the interpretation of a grant or transfer of land by the Crown.
predicates.grant_contains_no_revenue_free_term: The grant contains no term stating that the land is free from revenue assessment.
predicates.grant_does_not_otherwise_exempt_land: The grant contains no other term, promise or representation that exempts the land from assessment.
predicates.absolute_transfer_alone_does_not_exempt_: An absolute transfer, by itself, does not make the land exempt from assessment.

issues.definition: When a Crown grant contains no revenue-free term or other basis for exemption, its absolute character alone does not exempt the land from assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A tenure limiting assessment is extinguished when the land is acquired absolutely by the government and does not revive merely because the government later sells the land.
material_facts: The land was subject to a tenure limiting the assessment payable by its occupants.
The government acquired the land, extinguishing the occupants’ interests and vesting the land absolutely in the government free from the former tenure.
The government later sold the land, and the sale did not recreate the former tenure.
The legislation establishing the former tenure had been repealed before the sale, and no preserved right under it remained in respect of the acquired land.
issues.conclusion: The former tenure was extinguished on acquisition and did not revive on the later sale; the purchasers could not rely on it to limit assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Under section VIII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1857, the land vested absolutely in the government free from the occupants’ estates, rights, titles and interests, including the incidents of their former tenure. An extinguished tenure cannot revive merely upon a later sale. Section I of the repealing Act, 1870 saved rights already acquired or accrued, but no such rights remained in respect of land already acquired by the government. Collector of Bombay v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Bombay concerned a right acquired by prescription and did not establish that a tenure extinguished by acquisition would revive on transfer.

rule.if: land_revenue_assessment_dispute and government_acquired_land_absolutely and former_tenure_was_extinguished and later_transfer_did_not_recreate_tenure

predicates.land_revenue_assessment_dispute: A dispute concerns the government’s assessment of land to revenue.
predicates.government_acquired_land_absolutely: The government acquired the land and it vested absolutely in the government.
predicates.former_tenure_was_extinguished: The acquisition extinguished the former occupants’ tenure and its assessment-limiting incidents.
predicates.later_transfer_did_not_recreate_tenure: A later transfer did not expressly or otherwise recreate the extinguished tenure.
predicates.former_tenure_does_not_limit_later_asses: The former tenure cannot be relied on to limit assessment after the later transfer.

issues.definition: When an acquisition extinguishes a tenure and a later transfer does not recreate it, the former tenure does not limit subsequent assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A party may not raise for the first time on appeal a materially inconsistent contention that requires factual investigation unavailable on the record.
material_facts: The respondents had throughout the proceedings claimed immunity from assessment under the statutory provision governing the rights of superior holders.
On appeal, they advanced a new contention that they were not superior holders and that the assessment provision therefore did not apply.
Determining that contention would have required investigation of factual and legal questions for which the record lacked sufficient material.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the new contention and proceeded on the footing that the respondents were superior holders.
issues.legal_principle: The Court would not permit a party to change its position at the appellate stage to advance a contention inconsistent with its case throughout the proceedings when deciding it would require investigation of matters not addressed in the record.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is a civil appeal.
predicates.new_contention_is_inconsistent_with_case: A party raises on appeal a contention inconsistent with the position it maintained below.
predicates.deciding_contention_requires_unmade_fact: Deciding the new contention requires factual investigation that was not undertaken below.
predicates.court_declines_to_entertain_new_contenti: The court declines to decide the new contention.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, the court declines to entertain a newly raised, inconsistent contention when deciding it would require factual inquiry not undertaken below.

issues.legal_issue: A party claiming that land is wholly or partly exempt from assessment bears the burden of clearly and unequivocally establishing the limitation on the government’s assessment power.
material_facts: The respondents claimed that the land was wholly exempt from assessment or, alternatively, that assessment was limited by the former tenure.
The claim was advanced under the statutory provision governing assessment of land held by superior holders.
issues.conclusion: The respondents could claim complete exemption under the assessment provision, but the burden rested heavily on them to establish the claimed limitation clearly and unequivocally.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 permits a superior holder to plead that the government has no right to assess, as well as to claim a limit on the amount assessed. Under Goswamini Shri Kamala Vahooji v. Collector of Bombay, the person asserting a limitation on the government’s assessment power bears the burden of clearly and unequivocally establishing it.

predicates.land_revenue_assessment_dispute: A dispute concerns the government’s assessment of land to revenue.
predicates.claimant_asserts_limit_on_government_ass: A claimant asserts that the government has no right to assess the land or that its assessment power is limited.
predicates.claimant_must_clearly_establish_assessme: The claimant bears the burden of clearly and unequivocally establishing the asserted limit.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a land-revenue assessment dispute asserts a limit on the government’s assessment power, the claimant must clearly and unequivocally establish that limit.
